blocks.content: Judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution and cannot be abrogated even by a constitutional amendment.

rows: Narrower scope compared to US Judiciary
Wider scope giving judiciary broader discretion
Explicitly grounded in various constitutional provisions
Evolved judicially starting with Marbury v. Madison (1803)

items: Remember that the exact phrase 'Judicial Review' is not defined or explicitly mentioned anywhere in the Indian Constitution.
The 9th Schedule was originally immune to judicial review, but after the I.R. Coelho case (2007), laws inserted after April 24, 1973 are open to challenge.
Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue writs for fundamental rights, whereas High Courts under Article 226 can issue writs for both fundamental and other legal rights.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Judicial review is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders.
The term 'Judicial Review' is nowhere explicitly mentioned in the Constitution of India.
The Supreme Court declared Judicial Review as a basic feature of the Constitution in the Minerva Mills case (1980).
Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, and 227 explicitly confer the power of judicial review on higher courts.
The scope of judicial review in India is based on 'Procedure Established by Law', unlike the US 'Due Process of Law'.
